body:
A Society with Different Occupations and Resources

The population of the Mauryan Empire was socially and economically diverse. It included cultivators, herders, landowners, agricultural labourers, servants, slaves, artisans, merchants, officials, soldiers, religious specialists and communities living in forests.

Different groups contributed to the economy in different ways. Some controlled land or other productive resources, while others depended on wages, service or their own labour.

The Mauryan Empire was not a society in which all people had the same occupation, income or access to resources.

Differences Within Rural Society

Not all people living in a village were economically equal. Some households owned substantial land and employed workers, while others cultivated small holdings or worked on land belonging to someone else.

Descriptions of rural society in early historic texts distinguish several categories.

TermMeaning or association
Grama bhojakaInfluential village headman, often a large landholder, who could perform administrative and revenue-related functions.
GrihapatiHouseholder; in some descriptions, an independent cultivator or landholder.
GahapatiPali term for a householder controlling household resources; sometimes associated with wealthy landholders or urban elites.
Dasa-karmakaraSlaves and labourers who worked for others rather than independently cultivating their own land.

These terms belong to different linguistic and textual contexts. Their meanings can overlap, and they should not be treated as a fixed list of official Mauryan social classes.

The term grihapati or gahapati, for example, did not always describe a person of identical wealth or occupation. Depending on context, a householder might be an agricultural landholder or a prosperous member of an urban community.

Why Landownership Mattered

Access to land affected a household's economic security. A landholder could obtain produce from cultivation. Someone without sufficient land had to depend more heavily on working for others.

Large landholders could also exercise local influence because they controlled resources and labour. In some villages, the headman's administrative position reinforced his economic importance.

These distinctions help explain why an increase in total agricultural production did not necessarily improve the position of every rural worker equally.

Workers and Social Dependence

Slaves, servants and hired labourers contributed to agricultural, domestic and other forms of work. Their conditions were not the same as those of independent cultivators or wealthy householders.

The Arthashastra discusses the organisation and regulation of labour. It also describes penalties and obligations that reflected unequal social relationships.

Ashoka's inscriptions urged people to treat slaves and servants with consideration. Such instructions show that the treatment of dependent workers was a recognised moral concern. They do not prove that slavery or unequal working conditions disappeared during his reign.

Women and Economic Activity

Women participated in household work and productive activities. The Arthashastra describes arrangements for employing women in spinning and textile-related work.

Its discussion includes the supervision of work, the supply of materials and payment according to the quantity and quality of production. It also contains strict rules and punishments.

This is useful evidence that women's work formed part of the productive economy. However, the description is a set of recommended administrative rules. It does not establish that every woman in the Mauryan Empire worked under these arrangements.

Craftspeople and Merchants

Artisans such as weavers, potters, carpenters, blacksmiths and goldsmiths produced goods used in villages and towns. Merchants linked producers with customers in other settlements.

Economic success could make some merchants and artisans influential members of urban society. Associations or guilds provided one way of organising production and exchange.

Forest Communities and Herders

Many people within the empire lived outside large towns and settled farming villages. Herders depended on livestock, while forest communities used resources such as timber, honey, wax and forest produce.

Such communities could have different relationships with the state. Some paid taxes through established arrangements; others supplied resources as tribute or maintained a considerable degree of independence.

Religious and Social Diversity

The empire contained people who followed different beliefs and practices. Brahmanas, Buddhist monks and other renunciants formed part of its social and religious life.

The term shramana is associated with religious renunciants and traditions that included Buddhism and Jainism. Ashoka's inscriptions often refer to Brahmanas and shramanas when discussing respect, generosity and proper conduct.

Religious diversity was one reason Ashoka emphasised mutual respect. His instructions addressed the conduct of people belonging to different social and religious groups rather than prescribing one identical occupation or social position for everyone.

Limits of Social Categories in the Evidence

Megasthenes described Indian society through occupational groupings, while Indian texts used terms related to household status, occupation and social rank. These descriptions cannot simply be combined into a single, rigid system.

Moreover, descriptions of village society in NCERT draw on evidence from several centuries of the early historic period. They are useful for understanding the economic and social environment in which the Mauryas ruled, but each practice should not automatically be dated exclusively to Mauryan times.

Prelims focus

  • Grama bhojaka was an influential village headman in early historic descriptions.
  • Gahapati refers to a householder and may indicate control over substantial resources.
  • Dasa-karmakara refers to dependent workers, including slaves and labourers.
  • Women are mentioned in the Arthashastra's arrangements for spinning and textile work.
  • Shrenis organised important craft and commercial activities.
  • Trap: The occupational groups described by ancient writers are not all identical to the traditional 4 varnas.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 88–95; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'A Changing Countryside' and 'Towns and Trade', printed pp. 38–44; Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book II, provisions relating to spinning, weaving and labour, R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026; Ashoka, Major Rock Edicts III and XII, E. Hultzsch translation, Inscriptions of Asoka, 1925, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Mauryan Society: Landholders, Labourers, Artisans and Social Groups

body:
The State Was Both a Collector and a Supervisor

Mauryan government depended on the resources produced by the population. At the same time, it attempted to regulate activities that were important for maintaining the empire.

The Arthashastra describes state supervision of agriculture, trade, mines, forests, weights and measures and other economically important activities. It also discusses the collection of revenue and the management of resources.

These responsibilities were connected. Agricultural output supported the population and supplied revenue. Revenue paid for administration and defence. Roads and protected routes enabled goods, messages and officials to move between regions.

The economic strength of the state therefore depended on the productivity of its territory and the effectiveness of its administrative arrangements.

Economic Regulation Did Not Mean Complete State Ownership

State supervision must be distinguished from state ownership.

The Arthashastra recommends government oversight of many activities and describes state-managed farms and other productive resources. But ancient society also contained independent cultivators, private artisans, merchants and associations of producers.

Therefore, the existence of a superintendent for an economic activity does not prove that the government itself produced or owned every good associated with that activity.

Regulation and production are different functions. An official who supervises market weights is regulating trade. A state-managed farm is an example of the government directly organising production.

Ashoka's Dhamma and Administrative Policy

Ashoka's dhamma was a programme of ethical conduct that he promoted among the population. Its important principles included respect for elders, consideration towards servants, compassion for living beings and respect for different religious traditions.

The promotion of dhamma was connected with government because Ashoka appointed special officials and instructed existing administrators to communicate his message.

Dhamma-mahamatras were appointed to promote dhamma and attend to aspects of public welfare. Their appointment is recorded in Major Rock Edict V, which places the institution of these officers in Ashoka's 13th year after coronation.

Major Rock Edict III linked regular administrative tours with instruction in dhamma. This meant that officers were expected to carry out government business while also communicating the emperor's ethical instructions.

Public Welfare Measures

Ashoka's inscriptions also refer to measures intended to benefit people and animals.

Major Rock Edict II refers to arrangements for medical treatment for human beings and animals, together with the provision or cultivation of useful medicinal plants and other vegetation where needed.

Pillar Edict VII describes measures such as planting trees and digging wells for travellers and living beings.

These instructions show that the state could undertake activities beyond warfare and taxation. However, they should not be taken to mean that every well, road or irrigation structure in the empire was built directly by the emperor.

What Ashoka's Inscriptions Prove

The inscriptions are especially valuable because they record royal declarations and specific administrative instructions. They establish, for example, that Ashoka issued instructions to named categories of officials and appointed dhamma-mahamatras.

But an inscription giving an instruction does not automatically prove that the instruction was followed completely in every region. The scale of the empire and the diversity of its population make that distinction important.

The Relationship Between Agriculture, Revenue, Administration and Trade

The major elements of the Mauryan economy can be understood through their connections.

Agriculture produced food and other materials. Crafts converted materials into useful goods. Trade moved these goods between producers and consumers. Revenue transferred part of economic production to the state.

The state used its resources to maintain officials, soldiers, administrative centres and selected public works. In turn, government activity could help protect communication routes and economic centres.

This relationship explains why the Mauryan Empire needed both a productive economy and an organised administration. Neither could function effectively on the scale of the empire without the other.

Final Evidence-Based Distinctions

Common confusionCorrect distinction
Arthashastra and Ashokan inscriptionsThe Arthashastra sets out principles and recommendations; inscriptions record particular royal declarations and orders.
Bhaga and shulkaBhaga concerns agricultural produce; shulka concerns trade-related duties.
Samaharta and SannidhataThe first is associated with collecting revenue; the second with treasury custody.
Chaturanga and 6 military subcommitteesChaturanga names 4 fighting arms; the 6 subcommittees also include naval and supply functions.
Provincial and municipal administrationOne governs a larger territory; the other manages functions within a town.
State supervision and state ownershipGovernment regulation does not imply direct ownership of every productive activity.
Ashokan Girnar edicts and Rudradaman's inscriptionThe first are Mauryan royal records; the second is a later Sanskrit record that describes the history of Sudarshana Lake.

The Historical Significance of Mauryan Administration

The Mauryan Empire demonstrates how an early Indian state attempted to govern a large and diverse population through a central ruler, provincial authorities, specialised officials, taxation, military organisation and systems of communication.

Its economy depended on agriculture but also included towns, craft production, trade, monetary exchange and resources obtained from forests and mines. The state collected resources, supervised important activities and, in some circumstances, organised production and public works.

The strongest understanding of Mauryan administration comes from combining these facts with careful attention to evidence. The empire had a substantial administrative structure, but it did not control every part of its territory in an identical manner, and every recommendation in the Arthashastra cannot be treated as an established Mauryan practice.

Prelims focus

  • Major Rock Edict III refers to inspection tours by yuktas, rajukas and pradeshikas every 5 years.
  • Major Rock Edict V records Ashoka's appointment of dhamma-mahamatras in his 13th year after coronation.
  • Major Rock Edict VI concerns reports reaching the emperor.
  • Major Rock Edict II refers to medical arrangements for humans and animals.
  • The Mauryan economy included agriculture, crafts, trade, taxation and state-supervised productive activities.
  • Trap: An administrative ideal, a royal instruction and evidence that a practice was actually followed are 3 different kinds of historical claim.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 77–81, and Chapter 9, printed pp. 87–95; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 32–45; Kautilya, Arthashastra, Books II and VI, R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026; Ashoka, Major Rock Edicts II, III, V and VI and Pillar Edict VII, E. Hultzsch translation, Inscriptions of Asoka, 1925, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, 'Administrative and Institutional Structures', Unit 24, section 24.4, and 'Economy of the Mauryan Period', Unit 19, sections 19.2–19.4.]

title: The State's Role in the Economy and Society: Ashoka's Policies and Essential Distinctions
